chapter: Minton's, bop and the Monk circle
title: Being thrown out of clubs and jamming in New York
summary: Before Minton's, she and Dick Wilson, Lester Young and others opened clubs that threw them out once business was good; one jam spot beat a union delegate.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: What drew all this particular group of musicians to Minton's?

There was no other place to go except Minton's. They had been all over town. When I was with Andy Kirk I used to come to New York. Dick Wilson, Lester Young, some of the Count Basie musicians, and I - we'd go all over town opening up new places and the minute the business was going well they'd throw us out, wouldn't allow us to come in any more.
That doesn't seem to make sense. Man!
That's what happened. One time we were jamming in a club at 110th Street and a delegate was walking outside

saying that this is a non-union place. They said, "If you don't come out in a half hour I'm going to report you to the union." Dick Wilson stuck his head out and said, "Man, go ahead now because we're going to jam." We stayed there and went back the next day. We didn't care what he did because during that era everybody was just thirsting to play. You just had to play someplace. There was another club, private club, we opened up when Don Byas was with us on the jam session. It was a private club and there was about 3 people in this club when we first started jamming there. The place became packed and jammed. One night we went to jam and they wouldn't let us in.
No, I don't know the name of it.
Were you at Minton's quite a bit too?
How did it work out if Monk - did everybody take turns on the piano or -
Yes, they had the same idea that Kansas City had, you know. Several pianists were there and they'd take turns.
